newsitem.title: LEBANON: Lebanon's Hariri backs strengthening pound.
newsitem.headline: Lebanon's Hariri backs strengthening pound.

text.p: Prime Minister Rafik al-Hariri reaffirmed his support for the steadily strengthening Lebanese pound, saying that anyone who tried to speculate against the currency would lose heavily.

Hariri, who has backed the steady appreciation of the pound in his first four years in office, issued the warning at a weekend mass meeting with businessmen and politicians as he began consultations on forming his third government.

"Those who played against the Lebanese pound before lost millions of dollars and we know all these people. If they try to repeat this game they will lose even more," Hariri said in reply to a question.
"It is forbidden to play this game because it is playing with the life of the Lebanese people and we do not permit this game, absolutely, neither by big players nor by little players," he said.
The pound hit an all-time low of 2,825 per U.S. dollar just before Hariri became prime minister in October 1992. Since then it has appreciated steadily and is now 1,556.5 per dollar.

The Bank of Lebanon has maintained a tough policy in support of the pound, jacking up interest rates and accelerating its appreciation against the dollar in times of political uncertainty to penalise investors who took refuge in the U.S. currency.
Some Beirut bankers and economists say the policy of a strengthening pound is more political than economically based.

They argue that high interest rates on government treasury bills helping to maintain the pound are crowding out the private sector and contributing to a slowdown in economic growth and that the soaring public debt and chronic budget deficits are too high to support an appreciating currency.
